posts.title: Sleeping in a desert camp: what it's really like
posts.summary: No lobby, no key card, no wifi. Here's what a night in Erg Chebbi actually involves.
posts.imageAlt: Berber tents lit by firelight in a hollow between Sahara dunes at night
posts.body:
People picture either a luxury resort or a sheet on the sand. It is neither. Here is what the night actually looks like, so you know what you're saying yes to.

Getting there

The vehicle stops at the edge of Erg Chebbi, where the road runs out. From there it is about an hour by camel into the dunes. Roughly twenty minutes in, the last rooftop disappears behind you and there is nothing in any direction but sand.

The tents

Camp is a ring of black Berber tents set in a hollow between dunes. There are three options, and they differ in comfort rather than location — everyone sleeps in the same place, under the same sky.

  • Shared camp — a tent shared with up to four travelers, real beds and warm blankets, shared bathrooms. Included in the price.
  • Comfort camp — a private tent for your group with its own bathroom inside. €15 more per person.
  • Superior camp — a private suite tent with premium bedding, heating and a hot shower. €45 more per person.

Whichever you choose, it is a tent in the desert. That is the point.

Dinner and the fire

Dinner is tagine, served communally. Afterwards the drums come out. It is not a performance put on for a coach party — it is the crew, and whoever wants to join in.

The night

Two things surprise people. The first is the cold — bring a warm layer. The second is the silence. With no road and no town nearby, there is simply no sound at all, and most people lie awake for a while just noticing it.

Sunrise

Someone will wake you early to climb the dune behind camp. It is steeper than it looks and worth every step. Nobody has ever told us they regretted getting up.

posts.title: Classic Loop, Grand Crossing or Reverse Crossing: which route is yours?
posts.summary: Three routes, one desert. The right one depends on where you want to be standing on day three.
posts.imageAlt: A minibus on a mountain road crossing the High Atlas
posts.body:
All three routes spend the same night in the same camp in Erg Chebbi. What changes is where you start and where you finish — and that is really a question about the rest of your trip, not about the desert.

The Classic Loop — from €85

Marrakech to Merzouga and back to Marrakech. Pick this if Marrakech is your base, if your flight leaves from there, or if you have a riad holding your luggage. It is the one most people book.

The Grand Crossing — from €115

Marrakech to Merzouga, then north to Fes. One way, two imperial cities, and an endless desert in between. Pick this if you are working your way north and do not want to cover the same ground twice.

The Reverse Crossing — from €155

The same journey in the opposite direction: Fes to Merzouga to Marrakech. Pick this if you arrived in the north and are heading south.

What is identical on all three

Three days. The same camp, the same camel trek, the same sunrise. Transport in an air-conditioned minibus, pickup from your riad or hotel, and a group capped at 17 people.

What actually decides it

Where your onward travel starts. Ending in Fes saves you a long journey back if you are going north anyway; ending in Marrakech is simpler if you are flying home from there.

Compare the three on the booking page — you can switch route and camp and watch the total change before committing to anything.

posts.title: What's included in the price — and what isn't
posts.summary: The full list, including the things that are easy to leave off a brochure.
posts.imageAlt: A shared dinner laid out on a low table at the desert camp
posts.body:
A cheap headline price is easy. A cheap headline price that stays the same at the end of the trip is the harder part. Here is the whole list, both sides of it.

In the price

  • Transport in an air-conditioned minibus
  • Pickup from your riad or hotel
  • The camel trek into Erg Chebbi
  • Two nights' accommodation
  • Two breakfasts and two dinners
  • Berber music at the camp
  • The sunrise dune climb
  • Sandboarding on the dunes
  • Stops at Ait Ben Haddou and along the route

Not in the price

Lunches. We stop where the food is good and you order what you want. It keeps the base price honest instead of charging everyone for a set menu.

Drinks and anything personal. Bring some cash in dirhams.

Tips. Entirely up to you, and never expected.

Optional extras

You choose these when you book, and you can skip them all:

  • A camp upgrade — €15 per person for Comfort, €45 for Superior.
  • Quad biking — €45 for a single quad, €65 for a double.
  • Airport transfer — €25 one way, €45 return.

Paying

You reserve with 20% and pay the rest on the day of the excursion. Cancellation is free up to 48 hours before departure.

The booking page totals everything as you choose it, so the number you see before you pay is the number you pay.

posts.title: The camel trek into Erg Chebbi, hour by hour
posts.summary: About an hour on a camel, from the last village to the middle of nowhere. Here's how it goes.
posts.imageAlt: A camel caravan crossing the Erg Chebbi dunes in late afternoon light
posts.body:
It is the part of the trip people are most nervous about and most glad they did. If you have never been near a camel, this is what to expect.

Before you get on

The camels are already kneeling. You climb on while the animal is down, hold the front of the saddle, and lean back as it stands — back legs first, so you tip forward for a second. That moment is the only genuinely surprising part of the whole hour.

The first twenty minutes

You are still near the village. There are walls, a few palms, the odd motorbike. The pace is slow and you spend most of it working out how to sit.

When it changes

Somewhere past the first big dune the last rooftop drops out of sight, and the sound goes with it. No engines, no voices except your own group, just the sway of the caravan. This is the part people describe when they get home.

Arriving

Camp appears suddenly, in a hollow you cannot see until you're on top of it. Getting down is the reverse of getting on — lean back as the camel kneels.

Honest notes

You will be a little stiff the next day. Wear long trousers rather than shorts. Hold the saddle, not your phone — photographs are much easier once you've stopped.

If you would rather not ride, say so when you book. Nobody is put on a camel against their will, and we will arrange the alternative.

posts.title: Ait Ben Haddou, Todra Gorge and the stops people don't expect
posts.summary: The desert is the headline. These are the places travelers end up talking about afterwards.
posts.imageAlt: The kasbah of Ait Ben Haddou in golden afternoon light
posts.body:
People book this trip for the Sahara. They come back talking about the road there. Three stops in particular tend to catch travelers off guard.

The High Atlas

The first hours out of Marrakech climb through the mountains — switchback after switchback, Berber villages clinging to the rock, snow on the peaks into late spring. Most people expect a transfer and get a mountain pass instead.

Ait Ben Haddou

A fortified village of earth and straw, a UNESCO World Heritage site, and the backdrop to a long list of films. You can walk up through it. Go slowly; the view back over the valley from the top is the reason to climb.

Todra Gorge

The road narrows into a canyon with walls around three hundred metres high, close enough together that the sky becomes a ribbon overhead. It is cool, loud with echoes, and completely unlike anything either side of it.

And one more

If you are on the Grand Crossing to Fes, day three passes through the cedar forests of the Middle Atlas and Ifrane — a town that looks as though it was airlifted in from the Alps. It is the strangest thirty minutes of the trip.

None of these are extra. They are on the way, and they are why three days is the right length for this journey rather than two.

posts.title: What to pack for a Sahara desert tour (and what to leave behind)
posts.summary: Warm layers in the desert? Yes, really. Here's the honest packing list we send every traveler.
posts.imageAlt: A traveler's small bag and scarf resting on the sand at a desert camp
posts.body:
Almost everyone asks the same question the week before they travel: what do I actually need? The honest answer is less than you think — but the few things that matter, matter a lot.

The one thing people get wrong

The Sahara is hot in the afternoon and cold at night. Once the sun drops behind the dunes the temperature falls quickly, and the camp sits out in the open with nothing to block the wind. Bring a layer you would happily wear at home in autumn.

Every season, someone arrives in shorts and a t-shirt and spends the evening wrapped in a blanket by the fire. It makes a good story, but you'd rather be comfortable.

Bring this

  • A warm jacket or fleece — for the evening at camp and the climb before sunrise.
  • Shoes you can walk in — trainers are fine. You do not need hiking boots.
  • A scarf — for sun and for wind. You can buy one along the way if you'd rather.
  • Sunglasses and sunscreen — light reflecting off sand is stronger than it looks.
  • A small overnight bag — your main luggage stays in the minibus.
  • A power bank — electricity at camp is limited.
  • Some cash in dirhams — for drinks, tips, and anything you pick up on the road.

Leave this at home

A large hard suitcase, a hairdryer, and anything formal. Space in the minibus is shared, and nothing on this trip calls for smart clothes.

Why the overnight bag matters

You reach the camp by camel, so for the last stretch you carry your own things. Pack one small bag with what you need for a single night and leave the rest in the vehicle. It is a much better walk with five kilos than with twenty.

Still unsure about something? Message us before you travel. We would rather answer a question than have you buy something you'll never use.
